title: The Prince
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
setting: The Italy of the French and Spanish invasions, argued from Florence, the Romagna, papal Rome and the ancient world
lengthNote: A dedicatory letter and twenty-six short chapters, some of them under a page; chapters 3, 7, 12 and 19 are the long ones, and each is long because it is full of cases
openingLine: All states, all powers, that have held and hold rule over men have been and are either republics or principalities.
summary: A dismissed Florentine official sets down what fourteen years of embassies taught him about how states are won and lost, and sends it to the family that dismissed him. The book sorts principalities into kinds, tests each kind against a ruler who succeeded or failed, and keeps returning to one man, Cesare Borgia, who did everything right and lost anyway. Its notorious chapters on cruelty, fear and broken promises take up five of the twenty-six; most of the rest is about armies, and the last is a plea for somebody to drive the foreigners out of Italy.
referenceStyle: chapter, by the book’s own twenty-six numbered chapters; the opening letter to Lorenzo de’ Medici is cited as Dedication

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Prince, translated by W. K. Marriott
sourceText.note: This is a treatise, so everyone listed under characters below is a historical or legendary ruler whom Machiavelli reasons from, together with the author and the man he wrote to. Quotations follow Marriott’s English, which renders virtù variously as ability, valour and talent, so the word a reader expects is often not on the page. The opening line given here is the first sentence of Chapter 1; the dedicatory letter comes before it. The same file prints two shorter works after Chapter 26, which are not quoted.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: On his farm outside Florence, in the months after his dismissal, imprisonment and release.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: In Rome by Antonio Blado, five years after Machiavelli’s death; it had been read in manuscript for nearly twenty years by then.

atAGlance.label: Original title
atAGlance.note: Of Principalities: a Latin title and Latin chapter headings on a book written in Italian, and a title about kinds of state rather than about a person.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Kinds of state, then armies, then the prince’s conduct, then advisers, then fortune, and a final exhortation in a different voice from everything before it.

structure.label: Dedication; Chapters 1–5
structure.title: A gift from below, and a map of the ways a state can be held
structure.summary: Machiavelli offers Lorenzo the only valuable thing he owns, which is what he knows, and then divides the subject like a clerk opening a file: republics or principalities, hereditary or new, won by one’s own arms or another’s, by fortune or by ability. The long third chapter takes Louis XII through Lombardy error by error, and the fifth concludes that a conquered republic must be lived in or destroyed.

scenes.summary: The little volume is offered in place of horses and cloth of gold, with a closing reminder that its author is out of work.
Four sentences that lay out every branch of the argument to come.
Hereditary states are easy to keep; a prince of average powers will manage.
Annexed territories, colonies against garrisons, and the six mistakes by which Louis XII lost Milan.
Why Alexander’s successors kept Asia: the Turk’s kind of kingdom against the French kind.
Cities used to freedom never forget it, so the safe courses are ruin or residence.

structure.label: Chapters 6–11
structure.title: Founders, Cesare Borgia, and the men who rose by crime
structure.summary: The centre of the book’s case material. Moses, Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus show what ability does with an opportunity; Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia set ability beside fortune; Agathocles and Oliverotto da Fermo raise the question of whether success by murder counts. Then come the prince raised by his fellow citizens, the test of a state’s strength, and the papacy, handled with careful mock reverence.

scenes.summary: New orders are the hardest thing to introduce; armed prophets win and Savonarola did not.
Borgia’s rise on his father’s power, the execution at Cesena, and the one mistake Machiavelli will charge him with.
Agathocles and Oliverotto: cruelty well used and badly used, and the difference between empire and glory.
The civil principality; a prince needs the people more than he needs the nobles.
A state is strong if it can take the field, or at least hold a fortified town with a loyal people inside it.
Ecclesiastical states, and how Alexander VI and Julius II made the Church a power in Italy.

structure.label: Chapters 12–14
structure.title: Good laws and good arms, and why Italy has neither
structure.summary: Three chapters that the author plainly thought the most urgent in the book. Hired captains are useless if they are bad and dangerous if they are good; borrowed armies are worse, because they win for somebody else. Italy’s ruin is traced to a century of mercenary war fought so as to hurt nobody, and the prince is told to make war his one profession, in peacetime most of all.

scenes.summary: Mercenaries, the condottieri and their bloodless battles, and Charles VIII taking Italy with chalk.
Auxiliaries; Borgia’s progress from French troops to hired troops to his own; David refusing Saul’s armour.
The prince’s study is war: hunting to learn the ground, history to learn the models.

structure.label: Chapters 15–19
structure.title: How a prince must behave, which is not how he ought to
structure.summary: The chapters that made the name an adjective. Machiavelli announces that he is leaving imagined republics for the truth of the matter, and then works through the virtues in turn: generosity ruins a treasury, mercy can cost more lives than severity, a promise binds only while the reasons for it last. Each licence comes with a limit, and the limit is always the same: do not become hated or despised.

scenes.summary: The break with earlier writers: how one lives against how one ought to live.
Liberality consumes itself; a reputation for meanness is one of the vices that let a prince govern.
Cruelty and clemency, feared or loved, Hannibal’s discipline against Scipio’s mutiny.
The fox and the lion, Alexander VI’s oaths, and the need to seem to have the virtues.
Conspiracies fail against a prince the people esteem; ten Roman emperors are sorted by who hated them.

structure.label: Chapters 20–23
structure.title: Fortresses, reputation, secretaries and flatterers
structure.summary: Practical questions put to the rules already established. Fortresses help a prince who fears his people and cannot save one whom they hate; Ferdinand of Aragon shows how a run of great enterprises keeps subjects too astonished to plot; a prince is judged by the men around him. The chapter on secretaries is written by a man who had been one and would like to be one again.

scenes.summary: Arming subjects, fostering factions, building castles: the best fortress is not to be hated.
Ferdinand’s pious cruelty, the folly of neutrality, and the advice always to choose the lesser evil.
Three kinds of intellect, and the one test of a servant that never fails.
How to be told the truth without losing respect; good counsel comes from the prince’s own wisdom.

structure.label: Chapters 24–26
structure.title: Why Italy’s princes fell, what fortune can do, and a call to arms
structure.summary: The argument closes on its largest question. The Italian princes blame fortune for losses their own idleness caused; fortune is given half of human affairs and no more, first as a river that can be banked and then as a woman who favours the bold. The last chapter drops analysis altogether and appeals to the Medici, in the language of Exodus, to raise a banner and free Italy.

scenes.summary: Naples and Milan were lost by sloth in quiet times, not by bad luck.
The river in flood, men who cannot change their nature, Julius II’s lucky haste, and fortune as a woman.
Italy beaten, despoiled and waiting; the Medici urged to be her redeemer; four lines of Petrarch to end.

characters.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
characters.role: The author: former secretary to the Florentine republic, writing unemployed
characters.summary: He is present in his own treatise more than its reputation for coldness suggests. He tells a French cardinal at Nantes that the French do not understand statecraft, talks with Cesare Borgia on the day Julius II is elected, and ends the dedication with a plain statement that he is suffering undeservedly. The chapter on choosing secretaries is written by a man who knows exactly how good a secretary he was.
characters.clue: A civil servant of humble condition who says that princes are best understood from below, as mountains are best drawn from the plain.

relationships.label: offers the book and his services to
watched at first hand, and takes as his pattern of a new prince

characters.name: Lorenzo de’ Medici
characters.role: The dedicatee: Lorenzo di Piero, the young Medici then ruling Florence
characters.summary: He never acts in the book; he is the person it is trying to move. The dedication addresses him as your Magnificence and the final chapter addresses his illustrious house, and between the two he becomes the unnamed you to whom the advice on armies and cruelty is given. The treatise works as an application for employment made to the family that had its author tortured.
characters.clue: The reader the book is written for, who is promised greatness in the first pages and asked to free Italy in the last.

characters.name: Cesare Borgia, Duke Valentino
characters.role: Son of Pope Alexander VI; conqueror of the Romagna; the book’s chief modern example
characters.summary: Given a state by his father’s power and the French king’s soldiers, he set about making it his own: he broke the Roman factions, strangled his hired captains at Sinigalia, pacified the Romagna through a cruel deputy and then had the deputy cut in two. Machiavelli can find nothing to blame except the election of Julius II, and offers him for imitation although he lost everything, which makes him the test case for how much ability can do against fortune.
characters.clue: He planned for everything that might follow his father’s death except being at the point of death himself when it came.

characters.name: Pope Alexander VI
characters.role: Rodrigo Borgia, pope from 1492 to 1503; Cesare’s father
characters.summary: He appears twice, and the two appearances are the book’s view of the papacy. In chapter 11 he is the pope who showed what money and arms could do for the Church, though all he meant to do was enrich his son. In chapter 18 he is the supreme example of the successful liar, a man who swore more solemnly and kept his word less than anyone living, and was always believed.
characters.clue: He never did anything but deceive, never thought of doing anything else, and never ran short of people to deceive.

characters.name: Pope Julius II
characters.role: Giuliano della Rovere, pope from 1503 to 1513
characters.summary: An old enemy of the Borgias whom Cesare allowed to become pope, which the book calls the cause of Cesare’s ruin. He then serves three separate arguments: he reached the papacy with a name for generosity and dropped it to pay for his wars, he put himself in the hands of Spanish auxiliaries and was rescued by luck, and his headlong temper happened to suit his times so exactly that he never learned it could fail.
characters.clue: A pope who did everything in a rush and always succeeded, because he died before circumstances asked him to go slowly.

characters.name: Francesco Sforza
characters.role: Mercenary captain who made himself Duke of Milan
characters.summary: He is the first example the book names, and the cleanest case of a private man who became a prince by his own ability and then kept what he had won with little trouble. He is also a warning aimed the other way: hired by the Milanese to fight Venice, he joined Venice and took Milan, which is what a good mercenary does to his employer. His sons lost the duchy by avoiding the hardships of arms, and the castle he built made the family more trouble than any enemy.
characters.clue: A hired soldier who turned on the city that paid him and ruled it, and whose heirs lost it by preferring ease.

relationships.label: set beside, as ability against fortune

characters.name: Moses, Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus
characters.role: The four founders named together as the highest examples
characters.summary: They are always cited as a group, and the grouping is itself the argument: a prophet who spoke with God stands in a list with a Persian conqueror and two heroes of legend, and is said to have done nothing the others did not. Each owed fortune only the opportunity, which in every case was a people enslaved, scattered or discontented. They return in the last chapter, where Italy’s misery is offered to the Medici as the same opportunity.
characters.clue: Four makers of nations, one of them the lawgiver of Israel, who are credited to their own ability and to the fact that they were armed.

characters.name: Fra Girolamo Savonarola
characters.role: Dominican preacher who dominated Florence in the 1490s, executed in 1498
characters.summary: The one Florentine of Machiavelli’s own time to be given a place among the makers of new orders, and he is there as the failure. His order lasted exactly as long as the crowd’s belief did, because he had no means of compelling anyone once it lapsed. He is probably also the unnamed preacher of chapter 12 who said that Italy’s sins had brought the French, and who was right about the sins and wrong about which ones.
characters.clue: A friar who remade a city by preaching and was destroyed the moment the multitude stopped believing him.

relationships.label: the unarmed counterpart of

characters.name: Agathocles of Syracuse
characters.role: A potter’s son who became king of Syracuse by massacre
characters.summary: He rose through the army, called the senate and the richest citizens together one morning and had them all killed, then ruled securely for years and beat off Carthage. He is the book’s hardest case, because by its own tests he succeeded: nothing was owed to fortune, and the cruelty was done at one stroke. Machiavelli nonetheless refuses him a place among the most excellent men, and the refusal is the clearest sign that success is not the only measure in the book.
characters.clue: A king who owed nothing to luck and everything to a single morning’s slaughter, and who is denied glory all the same.

relationships.label: the ancient example paired with the modern one

characters.name: Oliverotto da Fermo
characters.role: Mercenary soldier who seized Fermo by murdering his guardian
characters.summary: An orphan brought up by his uncle Giovanni Fogliani, he came home with a hundred horsemen, gave a banquet, moved the talk to a private room and had his uncle and the leading citizens cut down there. He held Fermo for a year. The story is told in more detail than any other in the book, and it ends with him strangled at Sinigalia by a better deceiver than himself.
characters.clue: He invited the man who raised him to dinner, murdered him over a conversation about the Borgias, and was killed by a Borgia a year later.

relationships.label: the modern example paired with the ancient one

characters.name: Louis XII of France
characters.role: King of France, twice conqueror of Milan
characters.summary: He is the pupil who gets every answer wrong. Invited in by Venice, he had two-thirds of Italy at his feet within months, and then strengthened the Church, brought Spain into Naples, crushed his small allies, never came to live in his conquest and planted no colonies. Machiavelli counts the errors on his fingers, and the count ends in the rule that whoever makes another powerful ruins himself.
characters.clue: A king who took Lombardy quickly and lost it by doing the opposite of everything the third chapter recommends.

characters.name: Ferdinand of Aragon
characters.role: King of Spain; the living model of a prince who has made himself great
characters.summary: He is praised in chapter 21 as almost a new prince, risen from a minor king to the first in Christendom by keeping his subjects permanently amazed: Granada, then Africa, then Italy, then France, each enterprise growing out of the last. The praise is double-edged, since he did it all under the cloak of religion, and he is generally taken to be the unnamed ruler of chapter 18 who preaches peace and good faith and is the enemy of both.
characters.clue: A king who always had a holy reason for his next war, and never left anyone time to work against him.

characters.name: Septimius Severus
characters.role: Roman emperor; the fox and the lion in one man
characters.summary: In the survey of ten emperors he is the only cruel one who died in his bed. He marched on Rome under pretence of avenging Pertinax, bought off one rival with the title of Caesar while he destroyed the other, and then turned on the first. Machiavelli draws a careful conclusion: a new prince should take from Severus what is needed to found a state, and from Marcus Aurelius what is needed to keep one that is already settled.
characters.clue: An emperor who deceived one rival with a share of the throne while he killed another, and was feared by everybody and hated by no soldier.

relationships.label: offered to a new prince as the pattern for founding a state

themes.name: Winning a state and keeping it
themes.summary: The book is less interested in how power is seized than in why it so often fails to last. Its recurring image is the foundation: a prince who inherits has his laid for him, a prince lifted by luck or by someone else’s army must lay them afterwards, at risk to the architect and the building. Almost every rule in the book is a rule about making a new state behave like an old one as quickly as possible.
themes.development: Stated as a classification in chapter 1, tested on Louis XII and Cesare Borgia, and cashed in chapter 24, where a new prince who follows the advice is promised more security than an old family has.

themes.name: Fortune and ability
themes.summary: Fortune in this book is not chance in general but the world’s habit of changing faster than men do. Ability, which is the translation’s usual word for virtù, is the capacity to be ready for the change or to change with it. Machiavelli gives fortune half of human affairs and then spends a chapter showing that her half falls hardest on those who built nothing in calm weather, which shifts a good deal of what looks like bad luck back on to the unlucky.
themes.development: The founders owe fortune only an opening; Borgia is broken by an extreme malignity of it; chapter 25 tries two images, a river and a woman, and they do not give quite the same advice.

themes.name: One’s own arms
themes.summary: No subject gets more pages. A prince who depends on hired or borrowed soldiers does not possess his state; he is its tenant. The argument is military, but it is also the book’s theory of dependence in its plainest form: anything that rests on another’s goodwill, whether an army, an ally or a patron’s favour, will be withdrawn at the moment it is needed. Machiavelli had organised a Florentine militia himself, and these are the chapters where he sounds least detached.
themes.development: Announced in the last clause of chapter 1, argued through chapters 12 to 14, repeated in chapter 24, and turned into the practical programme of the exhortation in chapter 26.

themes.name: Cruelty, fear and hatred
themes.summary: The scandal is smaller than its reputation and more exact. Cruelty is well used when it is done once, for security, and then stopped; it is badly used when it grows. Fear is safer than love because the prince controls it, but fear is not hatred, and hatred is the one thing the book treats as fatal. The practical rule that follows is almost mild: leave your subjects’ property and their women alone.
themes.development: First weighed over Agathocles in chapter 8, made a policy in chapter 17, and tested in chapter 19 against ten emperors, where the ones who die are those who were hated or despised.

themes.name: Seeming and being
themes.summary: A prince need not have the virtues, but he must seem to have them, and religion above all. The reason given is about audiences rather than ethics: everyone can see a ruler and very few can touch him, so his reputation is made by people judging at a distance and by results. Machiavelli adds that it is best actually to be merciful and faithful, provided the mind is ready to turn when it must, which asks for a harder discipline than hypocrisy.
themes.development: Prepared by the staged execution in chapter 7, stated outright in chapter 18, and extended in chapter 21 to Ferdinand, whose piety is an instrument of foreign policy.

themes.name: What is done and what ought to be done
themes.summary: Chapter 15 sets aside the long tradition of books describing the perfect ruler and proposes to describe rulers as they are. The claim is not that goodness is worthless but that a man who insists on it among so many who are not good will be destroyed, and his state with him. Necessity is the word that carries the weight: the prince must know how to do wrong and use the knowledge or not as the case requires.
themes.development: Implicit from the first cold sentence about crushing men, declared as a method in chapter 15, and given its most uncomfortable form in chapter 19: good works can make a prince hated as surely as bad ones.

themes.name: The Church as a state among states
themes.summary: Religion is discussed only by what it does. Moses is a founder with an army, the papacy is a principality that needs no defending because ancient custom defends it, and Ferdinand’s holy wars are a way of raising taxes and keeping barons busy. The tone toward the Church is elaborately respectful and the content is not: the popes appear as the power that kept Italy divided and let the foreigners in.
themes.development: Louis XII’s first error is to enrich the Church in chapter 3; chapter 11 explains how Alexander and Julius made it formidable; chapter 26 borrows the miracles of Exodus to flatter a Medici pope’s family.

techniques.name: Argument by example
techniques.definition: Proving a general rule by setting out particular cases, usually one ancient and one modern.
techniques.inThisBook: Nearly every chapter states a rule and then produces a ruler who kept it or broke it. The cases are not decoration: Agathocles and Borgia strain the rules they are brought in to prove, and the book is most interesting where an example refuses to fit.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Setting two opposed terms against each other so that the choice between them seems to exhaust the subject.
techniques.inThisBook: The first chapter is nothing but forks: republics or principalities, hereditary or new, fortune or ability. The habit persists at every scale, down to sentences such as well treated or crushed, and it makes each conclusion sound like the only road left.

techniques.name: The maxim
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.inThisBook: Chapters tend to end on a sentence built to be carried away: men forget a father’s death sooner than a lost inheritance; whoever makes another powerful is ruined. These are the lines that travelled through Europe without the qualifications that surround them on the page.

techniques.name: Analogy
techniques.definition: Explaining an abstract matter through a concrete likeness that carries part of the argument.
techniques.inThisBook: A plain book saves its images for the places where reasoning runs out: the landscape painter, the archer aiming high, the physician’s hectic fever, the fox and the lion, the river in flood. Each makes a disputable claim feel like common sense.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.inThisBook: The grammar keeps sliding from a prince ought to you must. The shift usually comes at the hardest advice, so that the reader, and first of all Lorenzo, finds himself already standing in the position being described.

techniques.name: Objection and reply
techniques.definition: Raising the reader’s likely objection in the reader’s own voice and answering it on the spot.
techniques.inThisBook: And if any one should say, And if it be urged, Some may wonder: the manner is that of a man used to defending a policy in committee. It lets him admit the awkward case, Caesar’s generosity or the good emperors who were murdered, before an opponent can bring it.

techniques.name: Plain style
techniques.definition: Prose that declines ornament and claims the authority of the matter alone.
techniques.inThisBook: The dedication promises no swelling words or rounded periods, and mostly the book keeps the promise, which makes its departures audible: the mock piety about the popes in chapter 11, and the prophetic rhetoric of chapter 26.

quotations.text: just as those who draw landscapes place themselves below in the plain to contemplate the nature of the mountains and of lofty places, and in order to contemplate the plains place themselves upon high mountains, even so to understand the nature of the people it needs to be a prince, and to understand that of princes it needs to be of the people.
quotations.context: Machiavelli answers in advance the charge that a man of low condition has no business instructing princes.
quotations.analysis: The comparison turns his lack of rank into his qualification: distance is what makes a subject visible. It is politely symmetrical, and the symmetry hides a cost to Lorenzo, since it implies that a prince cannot see what princes are like and needs somebody on the plain to tell him. The job application is folded inside the theory of knowledge.

quotations.text: men ought either to be well treated or crushed, because they can avenge themselves of lighter injuries, of more serious ones they cannot
quotations.context: From the argument that colonies are better than garrisons, because colonies injure only a few people and leave them too poor to retaliate.
quotations.analysis: This is the first sentence in the book likely to shock, and it arrives as an aside in a discussion of costs. The reasoning is actuarial: the question is not what men deserve but which injuries come back. The either and or leave no room for the ordinary middle course of governing, mild unfairness, which the sentence identifies as the dangerous one.

quotations.text: in the beginning of the malady it is easy to cure but difficult to detect, but in the course of time, not having been either detected or treated in the beginning, it becomes easy to detect but difficult to cure.
quotations.context: Praising the Romans for dealing with distant troubles before they became wars on Italian soil.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a chiasmus, with cure and detect changing places, so its form acts out the reversal it describes. The medical likeness makes statecraft a matter of diagnosis, which suits a writer whose trade was reading situations early. It also prepares the book’s case against fortune: most disasters called sudden were visible once to someone who was looking.

quotations.text: he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined
quotations.context: The general rule drawn from Louis XII’s career in Italy, after he has helped the Pope into the Romagna and Spain into Naples.
quotations.analysis: A chapter of detailed Italian politics is compressed into ten words that would fit any century. The reason given is psychological: power is conferred by either cleverness or force, and the man who receives it distrusts both in his benefactor. Read from Lorenzo’s side it is an odd thing for a petitioner to write, since it tells a prince to be wary of exactly the useful servant Machiavelli is offering to be.

quotations.text: there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things
quotations.context: Explaining why even the greatest founders had trouble at the start.
quotations.analysis: The explanation that follows is an analysis of interests, not of courage: those who did well under the old arrangement fight hard, and those who may do well under the new one help lukewarmly because they have not seen it work yet. It is one of the few passages in the book about reform rather than rule, and it accounts for why reformers so often turn to force.

quotations.text: Hence it is that all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed.
quotations.context: Just before Savonarola is named as the modern proof.
quotations.analysis: Prophet is the startling word. By choosing it Machiavelli puts Moses, whom he has just said one may not discuss, under the same law as Romulus: the people believed because they could be made to go on believing. Florentine readers had watched the unarmed case burn in their own piazza fifteen years earlier, so the generalisation rests on something the first audience had seen.

quotations.text: The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed.
quotations.context: Borgia has had his governor Ramiro d’Orco executed and left in the square at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife beside him.
quotations.analysis: Spectacle is exact: the killing is theatre, staged for an audience that hated the deputy and needed to fear the master. The two participles name the two effects a prince wants from a single act, gratitude and awe, and Machiavelli reports them as a critic reports a well-judged scene. The cruelty was Borgia’s policy throughout; the execution lets him disown it and profit from it together.

quotations.text: he told me that he had thought of everything that might occur at the death of his father, and had provided a remedy for all, except that he had never anticipated that, when the death did happen, he himself would be on the point to die.
quotations.context: Machiavelli, then a Florentine envoy in Rome, recalls talking to Cesare Borgia on the day Julius II was elected.
quotations.analysis: He told me is the only moment in the chapter where the author steps into the scene, and he does it to certify the one thing no planning covered. The sentence runs through a long list of provisions and then trips on except, which is how the career went. The book’s whole dispute between ability and fortune is here as an anecdote: a man can close every gap but the one he is standing in.

quotations.text: Yet it cannot be called talent to slay fellow-citizens, to deceive friends, to be without faith, without mercy, without religion; such methods may gain empire, but not glory.
quotations.context: The verdict on Agathocles, after a paragraph conceding that he owed nothing to fortune.
quotations.analysis: Anyone who thinks the book measures everything by success has to get past this sentence. Empire and glory are separated, and glory is withheld on grounds that are frankly moral. The awkwardness is that a few chapters later a prince will be told to break faith when he must; the difference seems to lie in the triple without, a life with no restraint at all as against a ruler who does wrong only under necessity.

quotations.text: For injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.
quotations.context: The practical conclusion about cruelty well used, drawn from Agathocles’ long and secure reign.
quotations.analysis: Harm and kindness are both described as things tasted, so the subjects are imagined as palates and government as a matter of dosage. The balance of the two clauses makes an unsettling idea sound like household economy. It is also a rule about time, which is this book’s real medium: the same quantity of pain is a different political fact when it is spread out.

quotations.text: The chief foundations of all states, new as well as old or composite, are good laws and good arms
quotations.context: The opening of the military chapters, as the book turns from kinds of state to means of defence.
quotations.analysis: Laws are named first and then dropped within two sentences, on the ground that good laws cannot exist where there are not good arms. The move tells a reader what kind of book this is: law, the usual subject of political writing, is treated as a consequence of force. Foundations is the book’s commonest figure, and here the building is every state there has ever been.

quotations.text: he who told us that our sins were the cause of it told the truth, but they were not the sins he imagined, but those which I have related.
quotations.context: On how easily Charles VIII overran Italy in 1494; the preacher is not named, and is usually taken to be Savonarola.
quotations.analysis: A sermon is accepted and rewritten in one sentence. Sin keeps its name and changes its content: the offence was not luxury or impiety but the hiring of other men to do the fighting. The following sentence sharpens it by saying that these were the sins of princes, so the moral vocabulary of the pulpit is kept and pointed at a political class.

quotations.text: Francesco Sforza, through being martial, from a private person became Duke of Milan; and the sons, through avoiding the hardships and troubles of arms, from dukes became private persons.
quotations.context: Evidence for the claim that war is the only art that belongs to a ruler.
quotations.analysis: One family supplies both halves of the proof, and the sentence is built as a mirror: private person to duke, dukes to private persons. The father is in the singular and the sons are a plural, as if decline needed no individuals. It is the book’s case against inheritance in miniature; a title passes to the next generation, and the quality that earned it does not.

quotations.text: how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation
quotations.context: Machiavelli has just said he will depart from the methods of other writers and follow the real truth of the matter rather than the imagination of it.
quotations.analysis: The distance between is and ought is not denied, and it is not closed by lowering the ought; it is declared too wide to govern across. The argument is about survival, and ruin is its measure. What the sentence leaves unsaid is that a prince’s ruin is rarely his alone, which is the ground on which the chapters that follow will defend doing wrong.

quotations.text: Hence it is necessary for a prince wishing to hold his own to know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity.
quotations.context: The conclusion drawn at once from the gap between how men live and how they ought to.
quotations.analysis: Wrong is still called wrong. The sentence does not redefine evil as good, which would have been the easier and more comfortable course; it asks the prince to keep the ordinary moral names and act against them knowingly. Or not matters as much as the rest: what is recommended is a capacity held in reserve, governed by a necessity the prince must judge for himself.

quotations.text: it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
quotations.context: The answer to the chapter’s question, given after saying that one should wish to be both.
quotations.analysis: The famous half of the sentence is conditional on the second half, and the word is safer, not better. The reasoning that follows is about who holds the lever: men love at their own pleasure and fear at the prince’s, so fear is the only bond he controls. The chapter then spends as long on avoiding hatred as on inspiring fear, a limit that the quoted version always loses.

quotations.text: men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony.
quotations.context: Advice that a prince who must execute someone should do it with clear justification and never touch the property.
quotations.analysis: The joke is grim and the sentence works as a restraint. It tells a prince that confiscation is more dangerous to him than execution, since killing needs a pretext and pretexts run out, while a ruler who has started seizing goods never lacks a reason to go on. The low view of human nature is put to a use that protects subjects from the commonest kind of tyranny.

quotations.text: it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves.
quotations.context: From the passage on fighting by law, which is proper to men, and by force, which is proper to beasts.
quotations.analysis: Older advice to rulers had used the lion for courage and the fox as a warning. Machiavelli keeps both animals and makes them a division of labour, each covering the other’s weakness. The detail worth noticing is that the fox only discovers snares; cunning is presented first as a defence against a world of wolves and trappers, and the licence to break faith is drawn from that.

quotations.text: Alexander the Sixth did nothing else but deceive men, nor ever thought of doing otherwise, and he always found victims
quotations.context: The one recent example Machiavelli says he cannot pass over, in support of the claim that a deceiver will always find someone willing to be deceived.
quotations.analysis: The example chosen for successful lying is a pope, named without comment, in a book addressed to a family that then held the papacy. The exaggeration, nothing else and always, makes him less a person than a controlled experiment: a man who broke every oath and was believed at the next one. The lesson is about the audience’s appetite for being persuaded.

quotations.text: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are
quotations.context: Explaining why a prince must take care that everything he says seems full of mercy, faith, humanity, uprightness and religion.
quotations.analysis: The argument is about the senses. The many judge by the eye, the few by the hand, and the few will not contradict the many while the state stands behind them. This is a theory of public opinion written before the phrase existed, and the you makes it personal: Lorenzo is being told that he is watched by a crowd, and that the crowd’s verdict is the one that counts.

quotations.text: He who will, therefore, carefully examine the actions of this man will find him a most valiant lion and a most cunning fox
quotations.context: Summing up Septimius Severus, who deceived one rival for the throne while he destroyed the other.
quotations.analysis: The image from the previous chapter is given a body, and the body is an emperor who was cruel to the people and died in power. Machiavelli does not hide that, and he does not simply recommend Severus either: the chapter ends by telling a new prince to take from him only what founding a state requires. The example is offered as a kit from which parts may be selected.

quotations.text: always using religion as a plea, so as to undertake greater schemes, he devoted himself with pious cruelty to driving out and clearing his kingdom of the Moors
quotations.context: From the account of Ferdinand of Aragon’s rise, offered as the pattern of a prince who wins esteem by great enterprises.
quotations.analysis: Pious cruelty is the most compressed phrase in the book, an adjective and a noun that ought to cancel each other and are made to cooperate. The chapter calls the example admirable and rare, and the praise is technical, as one might admire a well-made engine. A reader is left to decide whether the coolness is approval or the driest kind of exposure.

quotations.text: So it happens with fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her.
quotations.context: The end of the comparison between fortune and a river that floods the plain but can be banked and channelled in fair weather.
quotations.analysis: The river does not stop being violent; what changes is where the water goes. It is the book’s most hopeful image and its most civic, since dykes and canals are public works and the next paragraph calls Italy a country without them. Fortune is still a she who knows where the defences are missing, so the flood keeps something like a will.

quotations.text: fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her
quotations.context: The close of the chapter, after Julius II has been shown succeeding by rashness because rashness happened to suit his times.
quotations.analysis: The second image of fortune quarrels with the first. The river rewarded patient engineering; this figure rewards violence and youth, and it arrives just after the admission that no man can change his nature to match the times. It reads as a preference asserted once analysis has given out, and its brutality is of a piece with a book that pictures mastery as force throughout.

quotations.text: God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us.
quotations.context: After listing signs borrowed from Exodus, the divided sea, the cloud, the rock and the manna, as omens favouring the Medici.
quotations.analysis: The miracles are produced and then told to stand aside, because the point is that the rest is up to the reader. It is the theology of chapter 25 restated for a devout audience: half is given, half must be taken. Glory, which was refused to Agathocles, returns as the prize, and the plural our quietly puts the author in the company that will share it.

quotations.text: To all of us this barbarous dominion stinks.
quotations.context: Near the end of the exhortation, after a run of questions asking what Italian would refuse a liberator.
quotations.analysis: After twenty-five chapters in the third person the book says us, and says it with the crudest verb it has used. The sentence is seven words long and follows a sequence of rising rhetorical questions, so it lands as a drop into plain speech. Whether the last chapter is the purpose of the whole or a flourish added to a technical work is the oldest argument about this book, and this line is the best evidence that the feeling was real.

timeline.label: Niccolò Machiavelli is born in Florence
timeline.detail: On 3 May, in the year Lorenzo the Magnificent took charge of the city.

timeline.label: Charles VIII of France invades Italy
timeline.detail: The Medici are driven from Florence and the republic is restored; chapter 12 dates Italy’s ruin from this unopposed march.

timeline.label: Savonarola is executed; Machiavelli enters the chancery
timeline.detail: The friar was hanged and burned in May, and within weeks Machiavelli was secretary to the Second Chancery of the republic.

timeline.label: Machiavelli is sent as envoy to Cesare Borgia
timeline.detail: He was with the duke’s court during the pacification of the Romagna and the killings at Sinigalia on the last day of the year.

timeline.label: Alexander VI dies and Julius II is elected
timeline.detail: Machiavelli was in Rome for the conclave; the conversation with Borgia reported in chapter 7 belongs to these weeks.

timeline.label: The Medici return to Florence
timeline.detail: A Spanish army restored them, the republic fell, and Machiavelli was dismissed from every office he held.

timeline.label: Prison, release, and The Prince
timeline.detail: Arrested in February on suspicion of conspiracy, tortured and freed in an amnesty, he withdrew to his farm at Sant’Andrea in Percussina. A letter of 10 December to Francesco Vettori says he has written a small work on principalities.

timeline.label: Giuliano de’ Medici dies
timeline.detail: The letter to Vettori names Giuliano as the intended recipient; the dedication as it stands is to his nephew Lorenzo di Piero.

timeline.label: Machiavelli dies in Florence
timeline.detail: On 21 June, weeks after the Sack of Rome and the second expulsion of the Medici; the restored republic had not given him back his post.

timeline.label: First printed editions
timeline.detail: Antonio Blado printed the book in Rome, with papal privilege, and Bernardo Giunta in Florence in the same year.

timeline.label: Placed on the Roman Index of Prohibited Books
timeline.detail: All of Machiavelli’s works were banned, which did more to spread the name than the reading of him.

timeline.label: Innocent Gentillet publishes his attack on Machiavelli
timeline.detail: The French treatise commonly called the Contre-Machiavel gave northern Europe a Machiavelli made of extracted maxims, and the stage villain followed.

timeline.label: Edward Dacres’s English translation is printed
timeline.detail: The first English version to reach print, a century after English writers had begun using the name as an insult; Marriott quotes Dacres’s rendering of Petrarch at the end of chapter 26.

timeline.label: Frederick of Prussia’s Anti-Machiavel appears
timeline.detail: A refutation by a crown prince who, as king, invaded Silesia within the year.

places.name: Florence
places.note: The republic Machiavelli served from the Palazzo Vecchio, and the city whose mercy to Pistoia and hold on Pisa supply some of his sharpest examples.

places.name: Sant’Andrea in Percussina
places.note: The family farm south of Florence, near San Casciano, where the book was written in 1513.

places.name: Cesena
places.note: The Romagna town where Ramiro d’Orco was left in the piazza one morning with the block and a bloody knife.

places.name: Senigallia
places.note: Marriott’s Sinigalia, where Borgia received his reconciled captains on 31 December 1502 and had them strangled.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Seat of the ecclesiastical principality of chapter 11, and the place where Borgia lost everything at the conclave of 1503.

places.name: Milan
places.note: Won by Francesco Sforza, lost by his sons, taken and lost twice by Louis XII: the book’s first example and its most frequent.

places.name: Syracuse
places.note: City of Agathocles, who seized it by massacre, and of Hiero, who rose in it by merit; the two appear two chapters apart.

criticalViews.position: The founding text of political realism
criticalViews.summary: The most familiar reading takes chapter 15 as the key: politics is cut loose from the moral philosophy that had governed advice to rulers, and judged instead by what preserves a state. On this account the book describes how power works and is no more wicked than a textbook of anatomy.
criticalViews.counter: The book does not stay neutral. It refuses Agathocles glory, praises and blames on every page, and ends in a sermon; a purely descriptive work would have no use for the word ought, which it uses constantly.

criticalViews.position: A republican’s book that does not mean what it says
criticalViews.summary: Because Machiavelli served a republic and defended republics at length in the Discourses, some readers have taken The Prince as irony, or even as a trap: advice that exposes princes to their peoples, or that would ruin a Medici who followed it.
criticalViews.counter: Nothing in the text signals the joke, the private letter of December 1513 speaks of the work as a serious bid for employment, and the advice to arm one’s subjects and avoid hatred is not obviously ruinous.

criticalViews.summary: Read from the last chapter backwards, the hard counsel becomes a means to an end: only a prince strong and unscrupulous enough to unite force in his own hands could expel the French, Spanish and Swiss, and the book is a manual for that one task.
criticalViews.counter: The exhortation differs so sharply in tone from the rest that it may have been added later, and the twenty-five chapters before it teach a prince how to hold a state, not how to free a nation.

criticalViews.position: An occasional piece written to get a job
criticalViews.summary: A more biographical approach stresses the circumstances: an unemployed expert, recently tortured, turning his dispatches into a gift for the new regime. The chapters on secretaries and on patrons of ability read as direct self-advertisement.
criticalViews.counter: A book meant only to please would not tell its patron that he who raises another is ruined, or choose a pope as its example of a liar. The occasion explains the dedication better than it explains the risks.

essayQuestions.question: Why does Machiavelli hold up Cesare Borgia as a model when Borgia failed?
essayQuestions.focus: Fortune, ability and the use of examples
plan: Set out the contrast chapter 7 begins with: Sforza rising by ability, Borgia by his father’s fortune.
Follow the measures Borgia takes to make a borrowed state his own, from winning over the Roman gentlemen to Sinigalia and Cesena.
Weigh the conversation on the day of Julius’s election, and the claim that only an extreme malignity of fortune undid him.
Examine the one error Machiavelli allows, the election of Julius II, and ask whether it undermines the defence.
Conclude on what a failed model teaches that a successful one could not, and connect it to the half share given to fortune in chapter 25.

essayQuestions.question: Does The Prince separate politics from morality?
essayQuestions.focus: Necessity, cruelty well used, and the refusal of glory to Agathocles
plan: Begin with the programme of chapter 15: what is done against what ought to be done.
Show that the moral vocabulary survives: the prince must know how to do wrong, and wrong keeps its name.
Use Agathocles, who gains empire but not glory, as evidence of a standard other than success.
Test the limits the book sets, the avoidance of hatred and the protection of property and women, and ask whether they are moral or merely prudent.
Decide whether the book replaces one morality with another, in which the safety of the state outranks the conscience of the ruler.

essayQuestions.question: How does Machiavelli’s way of writing make his conclusions seem unavoidable?
essayQuestions.focus: Antithesis, maxim, analogy and the address to you
plan: Start with chapter 1, where the whole subject is divided by either and or until only the new prince is left.
Look at how maxims close an argument and travel beyond it, using the sentences on injuries and on patrimony.
Consider what the analogies do that reasoning cannot: the fever, the fox and the lion, the river.
Trace the slide from a prince to you, and what it does to the reader’s position.
Set against all this the places where an example resists its rule, and ask whether the certainty is an effect of style.

essayQuestions.question: Is the final chapter the key to the book or a departure from it?
essayQuestions.focus: The exhortation to liberate Italy and its relation to chapters 1 to 25
plan: Describe the change of voice: scripture, questions, Petrarch, and the first person plural.
Find what chapter 26 inherits from the rest: one’s own arms, the founders, opportunity made by misery.
Consider the dedication and the exhortation as a frame, both addressed to the Medici and both about fortune.
Give the case that the chapter is a later or merely rhetorical addition, and what would follow if it were.
Reach a judgement on whether a technical book can be given a purpose by its last three pages.

discussionQuestions: Machiavelli says it is safer to be feared than loved, and immediately adds that a prince must not be hated. How much of the famous sentence survives the qualification?
Agathocles succeeded by every test the book applies, and is still refused a place among the excellent. On what grounds?
Fortune is a river that can be banked, and then a woman who must be beaten. Do the two images give the same advice?
The book is dedicated to the family that had its author tortured. Does knowing that change how you read the flattery?
Chapter 18 says it is best to have the virtues and be ready to abandon them. Is that a description of hypocrisy or of something harder?
Most of the modern examples are failures: Louis XII, Borgia, Savonarola, the Italian princes. What does a book of advice gain by teaching from defeat?

related.why: A close reading of the passage from chapter 17 on fear and love, with the qualifications the quoted version leaves out.
Written within three years of The Prince, and exactly the kind of imagined commonwealth that chapter 15 sets aside.
The English stage Machiavel at full stretch: a usurper who confides in the audience and performs piety between two bishops.
A study of cruelty badly used, by the book’s own definition: injuries that multiply with time instead of being done at one stroke.
Conspiracy from the inside, and a test of chapter 19’s claim that plots against a ruler the people esteem destroy the plotters.
